learningObjectives.title: Coastal processes and hazards: weathering, erosion, transport, deposition and landforms
Coastal hazards: mass movement and coastal flooding
Coastal management strategies: hard and soft engineering

questions.q: Freeze-thaw weathering is most active in which conditions?
options: Temperatures that repeatedly rise above and fall below 0 degrees C
Constantly warm, dry desert conditions
Ground that stays permanently frozen all year
Hot, humid tropical climates
questions.explain: Water in cracks freezes and expands by about 9 per cent, and repeated freezing and thawing widens the cracks until the rock breaks apart.

questions.q: Which of the following is a process of coastal erosion?
options: Hydraulic action
Longshore drift
Saltation
Deposition
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is erosion caused by the force of water and trapped air being compressed into cracks in a cliff.

questions.q: Longshore drift transports sediment along the coast in the direction of the:
options: Prevailing wind
Backwash
Ebb tide
Earth's rotation
questions.explain: Swash carries material up the beach at the angle of the prevailing wind, while backwash returns it straight down under gravity, moving sediment along the coast.

questions.q: Which statement best describes destructive waves?
options: Strong backwash and weak swash, associated with erosion
Strong swash and weak backwash, associated with deposition
Low waves with a long wavelength that build up beaches
Waves that only occur during neap tides
questions.explain: Destructive waves are high and steep with a powerful backwash that drags material back out to sea, causing erosion.

questions.q: Why do headlands and bays form along a discordant coastline?
options: Bands of harder and softer rock lie at right angles to the coast and erode at different rates
The coastline is made of a single, uniform rock type
Deposition is greater than erosion along the whole coast
Longshore drift removes all sediment at an even rate
questions.explain: Softer rock erodes faster to form bays, while more resistant rock is left protruding as headlands.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence in the formation of erosion landforms on a headland?
options: Crack, cave, arch, stack, stump
Stack, arch, cave, crack, stump
Cave, stump, arch, stack, crack
Arch, crack, cave, stump, stack
questions.explain: A crack is enlarged into a cave, then an arch, which collapses to leave a stack that is eroded down to a stump.

questions.q: How is a wave-cut platform formed?
options: Undercutting creates a notch, the cliff collapses and retreats, leaving a rocky platform
Sediment is gradually deposited at the base of the cliff
Rising sea level floods a flat area of low-lying land
Longshore drift builds up a ridge of shingle offshore
questions.explain: Erosion cuts a wave-cut notch at the cliff base, and repeated collapse and retreat of the cliff leaves a gently sloping platform behind.

questions.q: Why do constructive waves cause deposition?
options: Their swash is stronger than their backwash, so material is left on the beach
Their backwash is stronger than their swash, removing material
They carry no sediment at all
They only occur during severe storms
questions.explain: A strong swash pushes sediment up the beach, while the weaker backwash cannot carry it back, so material accumulates.

questions.q: Why does a spit often develop a recurved (hooked) end?
options: A change in prevailing wind or wave direction curves the deposited material landward
The sea level suddenly falls, exposing the tip
Hard engineering structures force the sediment to bend
Chemical weathering dissolves the end of the spit
questions.explain: A secondary wind or wave direction curves the end of the spit back towards the land, forming a recurved hook.

questions.q: At a beach, waves are low with a long wavelength, a powerful swash and a weak backwash. What is most likely happening to the beach?
options: Constructive waves are building up the beach through deposition
Destructive waves are eroding the beach away
The beach is being flooded by a storm surge
Longshore drift has stopped completely
questions.explain: These are the features of constructive waves, whose strong swash deposits material and builds the beach up.

questions.q: In which transportation process is material carried as dissolved minerals within the water?
options: Solution
Suspension
Saltation
Traction
questions.explain: In solution, dissolved minerals such as those from limestone are carried within the water itself.

questions.q: What happens during the process of attrition?
options: Rock fragments collide and knock together, becoming smaller and rounder
Rocks are dissolved by weak acids in the seawater
Waves compress trapped air into cracks in a cliff
Sediment is carried in suspension far out to sea
questions.explain: Attrition is the wearing down of sediment as pieces repeatedly collide, making them smaller and more rounded over time.

questions.q: After weeks of heavy rain, a cliff made of soft clay develops a curved failure surface and a large section slips downwards. Which process has occurred?
options: Rotational slumping
Hydraulic action
Longshore drift
Carbonation
questions.explain: Saturated clay slips along a curved (rotational) plane, a form of mass movement known as slumping.

questions.q: Which factor most increases the risk of coastal flooding during a severe storm?
options: A storm surge that temporarily raises sea level
A period of low neap tides
A sudden fall in air temperature
A reduction in wave height offshore
questions.explain: A storm surge, caused by low pressure and strong onshore winds, raises the sea level and can overwhelm coastal defences.

questions.q: Why does prolonged heavy rainfall increase the risk of mass movement on a cliff?
options: Water adds weight and acts as a lubricant, making slumping more likely
Water cements the rock particles firmly together
Rain lowers the sea level and exposes the cliff base
Water reduces the overall weight of the overlying rock
questions.explain: Saturated rock becomes heavier and the water lubricates slip planes, encouraging slumping and landslides.

questions.q: Rock armour, used to absorb wave energy at the base of a cliff, is also known as:
options: Rip rap
Gabions
Groynes
Revetments
questions.explain: Rock armour (rip rap) consists of large boulders placed at the foot of a cliff or sea wall to absorb wave energy.

questions.q: Groynes are an example of which type of coastal management?
options: Hard engineering
Soft engineering
Managed retreat
Doing nothing
questions.explain: Groynes are man-made structures built to control the movement of beach sediment, making them a form of hard engineering.

questions.q: How do groynes help to build up a beach?
options: They trap sediment being moved along the coast by longshore drift
They reflect all wave energy back out to sea
They import new sand from another location
They allow low-lying land to flood and form marshes
questions.explain: Groynes interrupt longshore drift, so sediment accumulates against them and the beach widens.

questions.q: A town builds a series of groynes and its beach grows wider. A settlement further along the coast, in the direction of longshore drift, then suffers increased erosion. Why?
options: The groynes starve the down-drift coast of sediment, leaving it less protected
The groynes have increased local rainfall totals
The groynes reflect waves onto the town's own beach
Sea level has fallen along the whole coastline
questions.explain: By trapping sediment, groynes reduce the supply reaching the down-drift coast, so its beach shrinks and erosion increases.

questions.q: A coastal authority with a limited budget wants a sustainable option that lets low-value farmland flood to create salt marsh and absorb wave energy. Which strategy fits best?
options: Managed retreat (coastal realignment)
Building a concrete sea wall
Installing rock armour along the shore
Constructing a series of groynes
questions.explain: Managed retreat allows the sea to flood low-value land, creating salt marsh that acts as a cheap, sustainable natural buffer.
